speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our economy has made considerable progress toward both goals over the past two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market has come into better balance, with continued strong job gains and a low unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased substantially from a peak of 7 percent to 2.7 percent but is still too high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are strongly committed to returning inflation to our 2 percent goal in support of a strong economy that benefits everyone.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Today, the FOMC decided to leave our policy interest rate unchanged and to continue to reduce our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are maintaining our restrictive stance of monetary policy in order to keep demand in line with supply and reduce inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Recent indicators suggest that economic activity has continued to expand at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Although GDP growth moderated from 3.4 percent in the fourth quarter of last year to 1.3 percent in the first quarter, private domestic final purchases—which excludes inventory investment, government spending, and net exports and usually sends a clearer signal on underlying demand—grew at 2.8 percent in the first quarter, nearly as strong as the second half of 2023.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Growth of consumer spending has slowed from last year’s robust pace but remains solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And investment in equipment and intangibles has picked up from its anemic pace last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Improving supply conditions have supported resilient demand and the strong performance of the U.S. economy over the past year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our Summary of Economic Projections, Committee participants generally expect GDP growth to slow from last year’s pace, with a median projection of 2.1 percent this year and 2.0 percent over the next two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, supply and demand conditions have come into better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Payroll job gains averaged 218,000 jobs per month in April and May, a pace that is still strong but a bit below that seen in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate ticked up but remains low at 4 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Strong job creation over the past couple of years has been accompanied by an increase in the supply of workers, reflecting increases in participation among individuals aged 25 to 54 years and a continued strong pace of immigration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nominal wage growth has eased over the past year, and the jobs-to-workers gap has narrowed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, a broad set of indicators suggests that conditions in the labor market have returned to about where they stood on the eve of the pandemic—relatively tight but not overheated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: FOMC participants expect labor market strength to continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median unemployment rate projection in the SEP is 4.0 percent at the end of this year and 4.2 percent at the end of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased notably over the past two years but remains above our longer-run goal of 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Total PCE prices rose 2.7 percent over the 12 months ending in April; excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 2.8 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The consumer price index—which came out this morning and tends to run higher than the PCE, PCE price index—rose 3.3 percent over the 12 months ending in May, and the core CPI rose 3.4 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The inflation data received earlier this year were higher than expected, though more recent monthly readings have eased somewhat.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Longer-term inflation expectations appear to remain well anchored, as reflected in a broad range of surveys of households and businesses and forecasters, as well as measures from financial markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median projection in the SEP for total PCE inflation is 2.6 percent this year, 2.3 percent next year, and 2.0 percent in 2026.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I are acutely aware that high inflation imposes significant hardship, as it erodes purchasing power, especially for those least able to meet the higher costs of essentials like food, housing, and transportation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In support of these goals, the Committee decided at today’s meeting to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 5¼ to 5½ percent and to continue reducing our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As labor market tightness has eased and inflation has declined over the past year, the risks to achieving our employment and inflation goals have moved toward better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economic outlook is uncertain, however, and we remain highly attentive to inflation risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve stated that we do not expect it will be appropriate to reduce the target range for the federal funds rate until we have gained greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So far this year, the data have not given us that greater confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The most recent inflation readings have been more favorable than earlier in the year, however, and there has been modest further progress toward our inflation objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will need to see more good data to bolster our confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know that reducing policy restraint too soon or too much could result in a reversal of the progress that we’ve seen on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, reducing policy restraint too late or too little could unduly weaken economic activity and employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In considering any adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate, the Committee will carefully assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our SEP, FOMC participants wrote down their individual assessments of an appropriate path for the federal funds rate, based on what each participant judges to be the most likely scenario going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the economy evolves as expected, the median participant projects that the appropriate level of the federal funds rate will be 5.1 percent at the end of this year, 4.1 percent at the end of 2025, and 3.1 percent at the end of 2026.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But these projections are not a Committee plan or any kind of a decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As the economy evolves, assessments of the appropriate policy, policy path will adjust in order to best promote our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the economy remains solid and inflation persists, we’re prepared to maintain the current target range for the federal funds rate as long as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the labor market were to weaken unexpectedly or if inflation were to fall more quickly than anticipated, we’re prepared to respond.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Policy is well positioned to deal with the risks and uncertainties that we face in pursuing both sides of our dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll continue to make our decisions meeting by meeting, based on the totality of the data and its implications for the outlook and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed has been assigned two goals for monetary policy—maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to bringing inflation back down to our 2 percent goal and to keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Restoring price stability is essential to achieving maximum employment and stable prices over the long run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our success in delivering on these goals matters to all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We at the Fed will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you, and I look forward to your questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So what’s going on there is that we had very low readings in the second half of last year—June through December, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re now lapping those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So as you go through the 12-month window, a very low reading drops out, and a new reading comes in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The new reading gets added to the 12-month window.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s just a, a slight element of conservativism that we’re, we’re assuming a certain level of—of, you know, incoming monthly PCE and core PCE numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re assuming, you know, good, but not great, numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And if you put that on top of where we are now, you get a very slight increase in the 12-month—in the 12-month, you know, reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just the kind of conservative way for forecasting things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If we were to get more readings like today’s reading, then, of course, that wouldn’t be the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s just a forecasting device.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think, I think—let me say that we welcome today’s reading and then hope for more like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah—no.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, I think we’ve, we’ve—what we said is that we don’t think it’ll be appropriate to, to reduce rates and begin to loosen policy until we have more confidence that inflation is moving back down to 2 percent on a—on a sustainable basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s the—that’s the test we’ve applied.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know that—I think if we—I don’t know that this rules that in or out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, really, it’s, it’s a forecast—a fairly conservative forecast month by month that would lead to slightly higher, you know, 12-months rates by the end of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If we get, you know, good—better readings than that, then you will see that come down or, or remain the same.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you’re at 2.6, 2.7 [percent], you know, that’s, that’s a really good place to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So as far as the SEP part of that is concerned—as you know, I talk to—I talk to all of the other participants on the FOMC every cycle, and we talk about their Summary of Economic Projections and, and the dot plot—and, you know, their dot plot and everything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And what you—what I hear and see is that people are looking at, at, you know, a range of plausible outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And in many cases, they’re—they’re thinking, “I don’t really”—you know, “I can’t really distinguish between two of these.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re so close for me.” These are very close calls, but we ask them to write down the most likely one—so they do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And as, I think, you’ve, you’ve—as you’ve said, there’s 15 of the 19 are, are kind of clustered around one or two.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think I would look at, at all—I’d look at all of them as plausible, but I’d look at—so I think that does tell you kind of what the Committee thinks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But what everyone agrees on is, it’s going to be data dependent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No one—no one brings to this or takes away from it that is on the Committee a really strong commitment to a particular rate path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s actually just their forecast and their—it’s a combination of their forecast and their own reaction function.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, again, everyone would say that this is very data dependent, and I don’t hold it with high confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think if you’re looking for—and, and don’t really think that they’re—they’re not trying to send a strong signal that “this is what I think is the right thing.” It’s just what they think at a given moment in time, subject to data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of, you know, future meetings, we haven’t, you know—we don’t—we don’t try to—we don’t make decisions about future meetings until we get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think in terms of what we need to see, I mentioned it earlier—we, we want to—we want to gain further confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Certainly, more good inflation readings will help with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not going to be specific about how many because, you know, really, it’s going to be not just the inflation rating—readings—it’s going to be the totality of the data: what’s happening in the labor market, what’s happening with the balance of risks, what’s happening with the forecast, what’s happening with growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, again, we don’t see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I—we do see today’s—we see today’s report as, as progress and as, you know, building confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we, we don’t see ourselves as having the confidence that would warrant—you know, that would warrant beginning to, to loosen policy at this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we—this happens too often, but it, it does happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It just is, you know—data came—I think it happened a couple of meetings ago—a few meetings ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So when that happens—when there’s an important data print during the meeting, first day or second day— what we do is, we, we make sure people remember that they have the ability to update.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We tell them how to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and some people do; some people don’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Most, most people don’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I’m not going to get into the specifics, but you have the ability to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that, you know—what’s in the SEP actually does reflect the data that we got today to the extent you can, you know, reflect it in one day.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we’ll, you know—you will see PPI tomorrow.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll know more about the PCE [inflation] reading as the month goes on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the initial CPI reading and its, you know, kind of first-level translation to, to PCE [inflation] we did have this morning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We were briefed about it, and people were able to consider whether they should make changes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, as I said, you know, some people generally do, but most people generally don’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So by, by so many measures, the labor market was, was kind of overheated two years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ve seen it gradually move back into much better balance between supply and demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve seen labor force supply come up quite a bit through immigration and through recovering participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s ongoing, mostly now through the immigration channel.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But still, we’ve had some increases in prime-age labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of on the demand side, you know, we’ve seen—well, we’ve seen quits moving down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve seen job openings moving down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve seen wage increases moving from very, very high levels a couple of years ago back down to more sustainable levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have seen unemployment creep up now sixth-tenths over the course of, of a year or so very, very gradually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you put all that together—what you have is still-low unemployment, still 4 percent unemployment—historically low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s moved up a little bit—it’s softened a bit—and, and, you know, that’s an important statistic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, but more than that, you’ve got strong job creation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You, you have payroll jobs still coming in strong, even though, you know, there’s an argument that they may be a bit overstated but still they’re, they’re still—they’re strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what we see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we watch the labor market, of course, and the economy as a whole—but the labor market very carefully—and that’s what we see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see gradual cooling—gradual moving toward better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re monitoring it carefully for signs of, of something more than that, but we really don’t see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So sometimes it’s—you can’t reconcile the differences.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You just have to, have to—have to look at it and, and try to understand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s why it always makes sense to look at a series, you know, in 6—in 3, 6, and 12 months of things rather than just one report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you’re right to point to the last report, where it was your—job losses in the household survey—job gains, big job gains in the establishment survey.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, I mean, we’re left with ambiguous results, and we have to deal with that uncertainty around data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nonetheless, the overall picture is one of a strong and gradually cooling—gradually rebalancing labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Job openings, while they’ve come way down, are still, you know, greater than the number of unemployed people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The jobs–workers gap is still a significantly positive number—greater than it was before the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, overall, we’re looking at what is still a very strong labor market but not the superheated labor market of two years ago or even one year ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The big thing that changed was the inflation forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the inflation forecast moved up several tenths for the end of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We had really, really good inflation data in the second half of last year, then kind of a pause in progress in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And what we took away from that was that it’s probably going to take longer to get the confidence that we need to begin to loosen policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we—there are—there are fewer rate cuts in the median this year, but there’s one more next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, so you really—if you look at year-end 2025 and ’26, you’re, you’re almost exactly where you would have been, just it—just it’s moved later because of that progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, you get another—you get data—different data today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ll have to see where the data light the way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’re, we’re—the economy has, you know, repeatedly surprised forecasters in both directions, and today was certainly a better inflation report than almost anybody expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ll just have to see what, what—what the incoming data flow brings and, and how that affects the outlook and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So two things about that—one, one is this—you’re right, it did move up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, but I want to remember to point out that the long-run neutral rate of interest is, is a long-run concept.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It, it really is a theoretical concept—can’t be directly observed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And what it is is the, the interest rate that would hold the economy at equilibrium—maximum employment and price stability—potentially, potentially years in the future where there are no shocks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s—it’s a little bit—it’s not something we observe today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Today we’ve got a very specific economy with all kinds of shocks we’re still getting over from the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s—I, I don’t think that the, the concept of r-star—it’s a very important concept in economics and in what we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, honestly, it doesn’t really get you where you need to be to think about what appropriate policy is in the near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I, I—back to your original question, people have been gradually writing it up because I just think people are coming to the view that rates aren’t—are less likely to go down to their, their pre-pandemic levels, which were, you know, very low by recent history measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, we, we can’t really know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s an interesting dispute and discussion to have now, but, ultimately, we think that things like the neutral rate are driven by longer-run, slow-moving forces.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, there’s a really good question about whether, whether those really have changed or whether, instead, rates and the economy are experiencing a, a series of persistent but, ultimately, temporary shocks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s been the debate, and we can’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But in the meantime, we’re making policy with the economy that we have—with the distortions that we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, my answer has been that policy is restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The question of whether it’s sufficiently restrictive is going to be one we, we know over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I think for the reasons I’ve talked about at the last press conference and, and other places, I think the evidence is pretty clear that policy is restrictive and is having, you know, the effects that we would hope for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’d be reluctant to try to draw that conclusion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, you can—you can translate it into the—into the language you’re talking about, but, to me, the focus is more on, we have a goal, which is price stability, and another goal, which is maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think we’ve got a good, strong labor market still.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think we’ve been making progress toward the price- stability goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then for a while, there was a pause.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s why we’ve been at this policy rate now for almost a year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, you know, it’s been coming—where’s it been coming from—let’s start with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, clearly a lot of what—some of what we’ve been getting is just the reversal of the—the unwinding of the pandemic-related distortions to both supply and demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that is, you know—that is complemented by and amplified—supported by restrictive monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So those two things have been working together.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve also had a very positive supply shock on the labor side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and, also, you get—you get a positive supply shock when the—when the supply conditions unwind and return to normal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’ve had, you know, above-trend potential growth and, and high growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And yet you’ve had the benefit of, of inflation coming down, you know, really fast, actually, last year, and you will see what the rest of this year brinks—brings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So these dynamics can continue as long as they continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and we don’t know that, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, look at today’s report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, if we see more like that—you know, we don’t—we can’t know what the future holds.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But in the meantime, we’ve made pretty good progress on inflation with our current stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, we think—we think policy is restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we think, ultimately, that if you—if you just set policy at a restrictive level, eventually you will see real weakening in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s always been the thought is that, you know, since we raise rates this far, we’ve, we’ve always been pointing to cuts at a certain point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Not to eliminate the possibility of hikes, but, you know, no one has that as their base case, so—no one on the Committee does.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But so that’s, that’s—you know, that’s how we think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what we’ve been getting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we’ve been getting is good progress on inflation, with growth at a—at a, a good level and with a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, ultimately, we think rates will have to come down to continue to support that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, so far, they haven’t had to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, that’s why we’re watching so carefully for signs of weakness.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t really see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We kind of see what we wanted to see, which was gradual cooling in demand—gradual rebalancing in the labor market while we’re continuing to make progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re getting—we’re getting good results here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: On housing—you know, the housing situation is a complicated one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you can see that’s a place where rates are really having, having a significant effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, ultimately, the best thing we can do for the housing market is to bring inflation down so that we can bring rates down so that the housing market can continue to normalize.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There will still be a national housing shortage, as there was before the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There will still be one, but the distortions that we see now with lock-ins and things like that—you know, low mortgages—in terms of banks, the banking system has been, you know, solid, strong, well capitalized.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Lending—you know, we’ve seen good performance by the banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We had the turmoil earlier last year, but, you know, banks have been focusing on bringing up their liquidity, bringing up their capital, and having a risk—risk-management plans in place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the banking system, you know, seems to be—seems to be in good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I, I think it’s true that housing—that inflationary pressures have come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we still have—we’re still getting high inflation readings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know—and I think you can see it in, in various places in—you know, in some parts of, of nonhousing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You see elevated inflation still—and that’s probably to do with—it could be to do with wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Goods prices have kind of fluctuated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s been a surprising increase in, in import prices on goods, which is kind of hard to understand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, may, may—we’ve taken some signal from that, but, you know—and, and, of course, housing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re seeing—you’re continuing to see high readings there to some extent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s, you know, catch-up inflation from earlier pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, I mean, overall, you’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflationary pressures have come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I mentioned, the labor market has come into better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Wages are still running, you know, I would say, above a, a sustainable path, which would be that of trend inflation and trend productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re still seeing wage increases moving above that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we haven’t thought of wages as being the principal, you know, cause of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But at the same time, getting back to 2 percent inflation is likely to require a return to a more sustainable level, which is somewhat below the current level of increases in the aggregate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think if, you know—if you look back in 5 or 10 years and, and try to pull out the significance to the U.S. economy of one 25 basis point rate cut, you’d, you’d have quite a job on your hands.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s not how we look at it—you know, really, the whole rate path matters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I, I do continue to think that when—you know, when we do start to loosen policy, that will show up in a significant loosening in financial market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the market will price in what it prices in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t—I have no way of saying—we’re, we’re not at that stage, so I don’t know what we’ll be thinking about at that time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s a consequential decision for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, you want to—you want to get it right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, fortunately, we have a strong economy, and we, we have the ability to, you know, approach this question carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we will approach it carefully while we’re very much keeping an eye on, you know, downside economic risks, should they—should they emerge.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we always want to avoid the tendency to dismiss the parts of inflation that we—that we don’t like and just make it go away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—but we had a quarter where inflation was running higher, and, yes, I could stand here and say, “It’s stuff we shouldn’t have taken signal from.” But it is what it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, you, you have to—you know, low inflation is low inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: High—so if you have a quarter where it’s higher—we tried not to take signal from the first couple of months, but we got a third month, and we said, “Okay, the signal we’re taking is that, you know, we think it’s going to take longer to get confidence that inflation is moving sustainably down to 2 percent.” That’s, that’s what we said.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think that was the right thing to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I still think that’s the right thing to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now we have today’s inflation reading, which is very different—very much more positive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to have to see what the trend is—what’s, what’s going to be the data going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re looking for something that gives us confidence that inflation is, is moving sustainably down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And readings like today’s, you know—that’s a step in the right direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, one reading is—isn’t—it just—it’s only one reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You don’t want to—you don’t want to be too motivated by any single data point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, you know—I, I don’t think anyone knows—has a definitive answer why people are, are not as happy about the economy as they might be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we don’t tell people how they should think or feel about the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s not our job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We—you know, people experience what they experience.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: All I can tell you is what the—what the data show, which is, we’ve got an economy that’s growing at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve got a very strong labor market with unemployment at 4 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s been a long time since we’ve had, you know, a long stretch of time with unemployment at or below 4 percent—very long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We had a period of high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We—inflation has come down really significantly, and we’re doing everything we can to—you know, to bring that inflationary episode fully to a halt and fully restore price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re confident that we’ll get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And in the meantime, you know, it’s going to be painful for, for people, but the ultimate pain would be a, a period of long, high—a long period of high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is people who—lower-income people—people who are at the margins of the economy who, who have the worst experience—who experience the most pain from inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, it’s for those people—for all Americans, but particularly for those people—that we’re doing everything we can to bring inflation back down under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, you know, I, I don’t have a precise date for you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But what we said is that we, we want to make sure that we’re confident that inflation is actually moving back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And when we are, then we can look at loosening policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So having that kind of confidence that inflation will be at 2 percent just—it just pays benefits to the whole economy, to all Americans, for a long period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We had that period for a very long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We very much want to get back to a place where people can, can not think about inflation—it’s just not a concern in the everyday economic decisions that they make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We were there for a long time, and our goal is to get back to that place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ve made good progress, and we’re just—we’re in the phase now of just, you know, sticking with it until we get it done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, encouraging has been that growth—you know, the growth, clearly, that we had last year, particularly the second half of last year, and we continue to see still-strong growth—solid growth this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s been very encouraging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you go back a year, there was a real concern about, you know, very much slowing growth and, and a recession—many forecasters had that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s not what happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Instead, we—the U.S. is, anyway, and it’s in—it’s in sharp distinction with many other advanced economies around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s been encouraging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would say that the, the—today’s inflation report is encouraging, but it comes after, you know, several reports that were not so encouraging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You asked about—your second question was really about shelter inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think if you go back a couple of years—we, we know that there were renters, and then there are, you know, people who own their houses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we have OER, which is owners’ equivalent rent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so when market-based rents go up sharply, as they did at the beginning of the—of the—when the economy reopened, they really went up sharply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those play into rollover rents much more slowly for existing tenants than they do for new tenants.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and so what we—so we, we’ve found now that there are big lags.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there’s sort of a—there’s a bulge of high past increases in, in market rents.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It has to get worked off, and that may take, you know, several years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nonetheless, as long as market rents remain—are going at—up at relatively low levels—and they still are—you know, this, this is just going to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It just is going to happen more slowly than we thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we, we also do sort of this thing where we impute a rental value to, to owned homes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s—you know, many countries around the world do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Some do it differently than us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s something that the—you know, that the, the price experts have regularly looked at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is not something that we’re the only country that does, and it’s not something we’re looking at changing or would look at changing, you know, anytime soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it—it’s true.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s one of the very hardest things in, in inflation and in prices is how to think about, you know, the services that someone is getting by living in a home that they could rent, but they’re actually living in it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And some countries—you should just ignore that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s not our—that’s not how we do inflation here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we do it the way we do it, and we’ve been very transparent about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, it’s true that we’re—we’re seeing delays in, in realizing what—what’s happening economically.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we understand that—you know, we understand that very well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we monitor all the things you mentioned and more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, what we’re seeing is, basically, spending was going up faster than disposable income during big parts of next year, so—last year, rather—and so what that—you’d expect to see is people spending more on their credit cards.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That—that has been happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Credit card balances have been going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Credit card defaults have been going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re not at high levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Remember that after the pandemic, people were cooped up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They couldn’t spend money.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They couldn’t go out to spend money; they could spend money from home.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But households were in very, very strong—historically strong—financial shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’ve now worked off a lot of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re, we’re watching that carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we see the same data that everybody else sees, but you’ve still got a household sector that’s in—that’s in pretty good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know—but, nonetheless, it’s not in the kind of shape it was in a year or two ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re, you know—we’re carefully watching that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So consumer spending is still growing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not growing at the pace it was growing at a year or so ago, but, but it’s still—it’s still growing solidly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, by the way, other parts of the economy are picking up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Spending on equipment and intangibles is—has picked up quite a bit, you know, in the wake of all the construction that we saw of new tech—you know, tech plants.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, overall, the economy is exhibiting solid growth, and, you know—something around 2 percent—which is—which is, you know, good—a good pace of growth for the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, no, you’re, you’re right, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we do see the same thing other people see, which is, you know, increasing financial pressures on, you know, more lower-income people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and, you know, the best thing we can do is, is to foster a very strong jobs economy, which we think we have done—ultimately to get inflation under control, because those people experience inflation, you know, very directly—very painfully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and, you know, once, once we get inflation under control, rates can come down—which, which will also improve things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know—you know, when I say “unexpectedly,” the first thing is more than, kind of, is in our forecast or in common forecasts—so, something more than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’ll be looking at everything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’ll—the, the labor market, you know, has the ability—has, has the tendency sometimes to, to weaken quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So waiting for that to happen is, is not what we’re doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’re watching very carefully; we’re looking at the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I always point out the balance of risks, so—and, and also the fact that we look at, at all of it—the whole situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, a decision to begin to—you know, to loosen policy could have several reasons associated with it at a given time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I, you know, I would just—you know, we monitor all the—all the labor market data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And if we saw troubling—weakening more than—more than expected, then that would be something we’d consider responding to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’d look at the—we look at the broader context of what’s going on, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I, I don’t actually have that kind of mechanical thing in, in my thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I get that, you know—as many good ones as we had bad ones—but it’s not like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s the whole.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s going to be the totality of the data—[including] labor market data, the growth data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of inflation, you know, you’d, you’d want to see real progress that builds your confidence that we’re—that we are on a path down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I, I don’t want to try to give you specific numbers of things, because that points to dates, and I, I just don’t think—we’re not at a point of being able to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we don’t—actually, it’s our—it’s our finance ministry, the Treasury Department, that has a responsibility for thinking about and, and, if it sees fit, doing things about the level of the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So for us, it’s just another financial variable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you’re right—the dollar has been—has exhibited, exhibited some strength over the course of the last year or so because the U.S. economy is very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t think of it as benefiting or hurting the U.S. We don’t—again, we don’t manage the level of the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s not our—that’s not our job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know—and for, for our economy, what, you know, we’re trying to foster is maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we feel like we’ve made good progress on, on both of those goals over the course of the past year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know—so we are—we’re well aware of the two-sided risks here, let me just say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we understand that if we wait too long, that could come at the cost of economic activity, of employment, of the expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that if we move too, too quickly, we could end up undoing a lot of the good that we’ve done and have to then start over, and it could be very disruptive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re, we’re extremely aware of both of those risks and, and just basically trying to manage them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And what we said is that we’ll—that we’re—we don’t think it’ll be appropriate to, to begin to loosen policy until we’re more confident that inflation is moving down to 2 percent over time on a sustainable basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s—that’s kind of been our test.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Or there’s another test, which is, you know, an unexpected deterioration in labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think that’s, that’s the right way for us to think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s our—that’s our dual mandate there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we, we have a strong economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve got growth—all forecasts are very commonly around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s a—that’s a strong growth rate for our economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market continues to print jobs at a pretty high rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Unemployment is still low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we have the ability now to approach this question carefully, and that’s, that’s what we’re doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, we, we completely understand that that’s the risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s, that’s not what we’re—that’s not our plan is to wait for things to break and then try to fix them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re, we’re trying to balance these two goals in a way that is consistent with our framework, and we think we’re doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we—what, what we’ve been thinking is that we would announce and commence the review later or late in the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the meantime, as that time approaches, we will be devoting a lot of careful thought and planning to the contours of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Within scope would certainly be communications generally.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I—I’m not going to say that we’ll look at this or that particular thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And all the other details, you know—we’re just—we don’t want to get prematurely into a conversation until it’s really time to have it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so, you know, I’m going to leave pretty much everything else to, to later in the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t—there isn’t any one thing—one variable, like housing prices moderating, that would really decide or decide against what we’re doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve got an overall test, which is greater confidence that inflation is moving down to 2 percent on a sustainable basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s our overall test.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Or, alternatively, we see unexpected weakening in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So those are—those are two different tests.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would say, you know, we’re not—we’re not looking at any one price in any one sector and saying, “That’s the one.” We don’t target housing prices, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we don’t target wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we target aggregate prices and overall employment, so— NANCY MARSHALL-GENZER.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Any price that contributed to ongoing disinflation would matter, too, but I wouldn’t single out housing as having a, a special role there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you very much.
